headline_findings: This comparison covers two papers - one on Lyme disease and one on Long COVID - and does not describe either condition in general.

The Lyme disease paper reports a quantified gap between a claims-based diagnosis estimate (about 476,000 patients/year, 95% credible interval 405,000-547,000) and official surveillance counts (about 35,000 cases/year, with a general range of 30,000-40,000/year stated elsewhere in the paper), while the Long COVID paper instead shows a demographic and socioeconomic skew in who receives the U09.9 diagnosis code rather than a comparable national count gap.
Neither paper contains any direct medical cost, out-of-pocket cost, lost-income, or caregiving-burden figures, so this comparison cannot speak to the dollar cost of either condition.

comparison_rows.dimension: Scale of the gap between official counts and diagnosis-pattern estimates

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper estimates about 476,000 patients/year were diagnosed and treated based on commercial insurance claims, compared with about 35,000 cases/year reported through official surveillance (a general range of 30,000-40,000/year is also given), and states the gap reflects an unseparated mix of real underreporting and clinical overdiagnosis.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper does not produce a comparable national count-versus-surveillance gap figure; instead it reports that 37.2% of the U09.9-coded cohort had no recorded acute COVID-19 test, pointing to undocumented or external testing rather than a quantified national undercount multiple.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: The two papers measure undercounting in structurally different ways, so a reader should not treat their figures as interchangeable estimates of the same gap.

comparison_rows.dimension: Delay between symptom onset and formal diagnostic recognition

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports no data on diagnostic delay or time to diagnosis for individual patients.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper reports an approximate 2-year delay between when patients began describing long COVID symptoms and when a dedicated ICD-10-CM code (U09.9) became available, which it states potentially left many earlier patients uncoded.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Only the Long COVID paper provides evidence on a specific, named delay affecting diagnostic recognition.

comparison_rows.dimension: Demographic or socioeconomic skew in who gets diagnosed or coded

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper presents its diagnosis estimates only as single pooled national figures, with no breakdown by sex, race, ethnicity, or other subgroup given in the paper itself.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper reports that the U09.9-coded cohort was 11.3 percentage points more female and 10.7 percentage points more White than the comparator group of all SARS-CoV-2-positive patients at the same sites, and was underrepresented in higher-poverty, higher-unemployment, and higher-public-insurance-reliance ZIP code areas.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Only the Long COVID paper offers concrete evidence of who is more or less likely to be captured by official diagnosis codes.

comparison_rows.dimension: Out-of-pocket or direct medical cost evidence

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports no dollar cost figures of any kind, direct or out-of-pocket.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper also reports no dollar cost figures of any kind, direct or out-of-pocket.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Neither paper can support a cost-of-illness estimate on its own, which limits any financial-burden comparison across the two conditions.

comparison_rows.dimension: Work and income loss, and caregiving burden

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports no data on lost income, productivity, or caregiving time.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper reports no data on lost income, productivity, or caregiving time.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Both papers leave the indirect economic burden of the condition entirely unmeasured.

comparison_rows.dimension: Access barriers linked to diagnosis or coding

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper notes its underlying claims data source 'might not be representative of the US population with respect to disease risk and access to health care' but does not quantify any access barrier, and its data covers only privately insured residents under 65.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper reports that U09.9-coded patients were underrepresented in areas with higher poverty, higher unemployment, and higher reliance on public health insurance, despite those areas having higher COVID-19 case and death rates, and states patients in more socially deprived areas 'may be less likely to receive a U09.9 code in a healthcare setting.'

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Only the Long COVID paper directly links area-level socioeconomic measures to the chance of being diagnostically captured.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper's estimate is built entirely from commercial insurance claims identified by an ICD diagnosis code plus a qualifying antibiotic prescription, with an explicit correction factor applied because medical records frequently lack the specific Lyme billing code.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper's cohort is built entirely from an EHR-recorded ICD-10-CM diagnosis code (U09.9), and the paper notes clinicians' inconsistent application of that code creates a disconnect between coding guidance and actual billing practice.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Both estimates rest on administrative diagnosis or billing codes rather than direct clinical confirmation, which each paper itself flags as a source of produce lower or different counts in the setting studied.

comparison_rows.dimension: What the evidence leaves unmeasured about outcomes and duration

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports no data on treatment duration, treatment outcomes, or persistent-symptom prevalence.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper reports care-utilization figures only within a 60-day post-diagnosis window (for example, 22.8% with imaging) and states it cannot support any longer-term or multi-year outcome projection without added assumptions.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Neither paper can describe how the condition or its burden evolves beyond its own short observation window.

shared_themes.theme: Both papers build their entire diagnosis-frequency evidence from administrative diagnosis or billing codes, and both explicitly state this produces lower or different counts in the setting studied.

evidence.note: The Lyme disease paper applies a 2.33x correction factor because medical records often lack the specific Lyme billing code even when surveillance criteria are met.

The Long COVID paper finds the U09.9-coded cohort skews demographically and geographically compared to all SARS-CoV-2-positive patients at the same sites, which it attributes to disparities in who gets coded.

shared_themes.theme: Both papers report no direct medical cost, non-medical cost, lost income, or caregiving-time figures, meaning neither can support a dollar burden estimate on its own.

evidence.note: The Lyme disease paper is described as a pure case-frequency/diagnosis-count study with no cost data of any kind.
The Long COVID paper's burden evidence is limited to diagnostic/coding patterns and care-utilization percentages, with no dollar figures reported.

shared_themes.theme: Both papers describe a systemic coding or surveillance infrastructure gap rather than attributing undercounting to patient behavior alone.

evidence.note: The Lyme disease paper states that evolving electronic medical and laboratory systems should help fill demonstrable data gaps in Lyme coding.
The Long COVID paper quotes a CDC Q&A attendee noting 'physicians don't speak coding,' illustrating a disconnect between coding guidance and clinical billing practice.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Lyme disease paper quantifies a large multiple-fold gap between a claims-based diagnosis estimate and the official surveillance count, while stating this gap cannot be cleanly separated into underreporting versus overdiagnosis.

evidence.note: Estimated 476,000 diagnosed-and-treated patients/year compares against roughly 35,000 cases/year captured by surveillance, per this paper's own figures.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Lyme disease paper's estimate is restricted to a privately insured population under 65, limiting how far its national diagnosis-frequency figure can be generalized.

evidence.note: The underlying MarketScan claims data cover only privately insured US residents younger than 65, excluding Medicare, Medicaid, and uninsured populations.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Long COVID paper documents a specific demographic and area-level socioeconomic skew in who receives a formal diagnosis code.

evidence.note: The U09.9-coded cohort was 11.3 percentage points more female and 10.7 percentage points more White than the comparator cohort of all SARS-CoV-2-positive patients at the same sites.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Long COVID paper identifies a specific multi-year delay between patient-reported symptom onset and the availability of a dedicated diagnosis code.

evidence.note: The paper states the ICD-10-CM code U09.9 was not released until nearly two years after patients began describing long COVID symptoms.

evidence_gaps_shared: Neither paper reports direct medical costs, non-medical costs, lost income, or caregiving-time data, so no dollar burden figure can be built from either paper alone.

Neither paper provides a full subgroup breakdown of its core frequency or utilization figures: the Lyme disease paper presents only pooled national figures, and the Long COVID paper reports demographic skew in who is coded but does not break down its care-utilization percentages by subgroup.
cross_analysis.summary: This comparison covers exactly two already-generated simulators - one built from a Lyme disease paper and one built from a Long COVID paper - and is not a controlled study of either condition. Both papers focus on how official diagnosis or surveillance counts compare to broader diagnosis-pattern data drawn from claims or EHR codes, but they measure this in different ways: the Lyme disease paper gives a specific numeric gap between a claims-based estimate and surveillance counts, while the Long COVID paper shows demographic and socioeconomic skew in who receives a diagnosis code plus a multi-year delay in that code's availability. Neither paper contains any cost, income-loss, or caregiving-burden data, so this comparison cannot address the financial burden of either condition. The patterns described here reflect only what these two specific uploaded documents report, not the conditions in general.
cross_analysis.limitations: This is a small, non-random sample based on whichever documents happened to be uploaded: exactly one Lyme disease paper and one Long COVID paper, with no cross-condition or other-category papers available, and no controlled comparison was performed.

learning_cards.headline: Measuring the exact size of a diagnosis gap, not just its skew
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Lyme disease paper reports a claims-based estimate of 477650 patients/year diagnosed and treated, which is 442650 patients/year higher than surveillance-reported counts.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Long COVID paper describes who is over- or under-represented among coded patients but does not give a single overall number estimating how many Long COVID cases exist beyond the U09.9-coded cohort.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Long COVID researchers calculate a similar claims-based-versus-surveillance gap number for U09.9 diagnoses, the way the Lyme disease paper did?

learning_cards.headline: Checking whether diagnoses cluster in unexpected places
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Lyme disease paper finds that the claims-based estimate is 14 percentage points more concentrated in low-incidence states than surveillance-reported cases.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Long COVID paper does not report any geographic breakdown of where U09.9-coded patients are located relative to case burden.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Is U09.9 coding also more common in certain regions than expected, the way claims-based Lyme diagnoses skew toward low-incidence states?

learning_cards.headline: Checking who actually gets the diagnosis, not just how many
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Long COVID paper finds the U09.9 cohort is 11.3 percentage points more female and 10.7 percentage points more White than the comparator group.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Lyme disease paper reports an overall numeric gap between claims-based and surveillance counts but does not break this down by sex or race.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Does the Lyme disease claims-based estimate also show demographic skew by sex or race compared with surveillance-reported cases?

learning_cards.headline: Asking whether diagnoses come with confirmed testing
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Long COVID paper finds that 37.2% of the U09.9 cohort has no recorded acute COVID-19 test.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Lyme disease paper does not report what share of its claims-based diagnosed-and-treated estimate had documented laboratory confirmation.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: What proportion of the Lyme disease claims-based estimate lacks a documented confirmatory test, similar to the untested share found in Long COVID coding?

learning.takeaway: The Lyme disease paper's approach of calculating a single numeric and geographic gap could prompt similar calculations for Long COVID coding, while the Long COVID paper's demographic and testing-confirmation breakdowns could prompt similar questions about who gets counted in the Lyme disease claims-based estimate.
